claims.text: The proposed approach separately models phonon and electronic heat transport using first-principles calculations and temperature-dependent phonon Boltzmann transport.
The proposed approach will predict total thermal conductivity more accurately than prior Debye-based or perfect-lattice estimates.
The improvement in agreement with measurements will be roughly 20%.
The target material is nominally equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr containing approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
The modeled specimen is a dense, single-phase polycrystalline bulk with minimal porosity and second-phase inclusions.
The framework incorporates separate scattering channels for non-idealities such as oxygen impurities.
Atomic-scale chemical disorder produces scattering that affects heat transport.
Oxygen acts as a point-defect scatterer in HfNbTaTiZr.
Disorder and oxygen point defects influence both phonon and electron transport pathways.
Explicitly decoupling lattice and electronic contributions allows complex scattering mechanisms and local structural disorder to be represented more accurately.
Representing those mechanisms will lead to more accurate total thermal-conductivity predictions.
Predicted total thermal conductivity will remain within ±2 W/(K·m) of measurements from 200 to 1200 K.
The approach will isolate lattice and electronic contributions better than established single-parameter or ideal-lattice models.
Earlier Debye-based or defect-free bulk-crystal simulations often differ from experimental results by at least 30%.
Earlier models do not correctly partition lattice and electronic thermal conduction.
The approach is applicable primarily to homogeneous, single-phase HfNbTaTiZr containing no more than approximately 1 wt.% oxygen between 200 and 1200 K.
Higher impurity concentrations or substantial microstructural heterogeneity would require model refinement.
Grain boundaries and second phases may introduce scattering contributions not captured adequately without additional experimental data.
